"Well, gosh! I never could put on airs," Leo replied, enjoying the way her fingers now played with the collar of his linen shirt. "I just think I'm a pretty ordinary fellow who came in for an extraordinary line of luck. I would have made a pretty good bluff at building fences or fixing engines, or any sort of honest work; as it was, when I was a youngster, growing up, I used to say to myself, 'You think you're going to be a grand engineer, but half the successful men in the world are born with all the connections, anything may happen!' Some minds are just naturally better for it than others, and his was, and mine is. And at twenty-five I came of age, and found that my prospects were pretty safely fixed, and that Grandfather was kind of counting on my going in with his firm. So there you are! Things just come my way; as I say, I'd have been satisfied with less, but I've got in the habit of taking my luck for granted."

"And some, like myself," she added, brightening, "are born in the dusty corners, and push into the light! And we're the really lucky ones! Eleanor took immense pleasure in the domestic details, in arranging her small kitchen, in ensuring every corner of their new dwelling felt comfortable and welcoming. It was a tangible manifestation of their dreams, a haven in the bustling city.

One evening, after a particularly demanding day at the factory, Leo returned home to find Eleanor preparing a simple, but delicious, supper of roasted chicken and fresh green beans. The apartment was filled with the comforting aromas of home cooking, and the soft glow of the gaslight cast a warm, intimate light on the parlor. He shed his coat, loosened his tie, and sank into the armchair Arthur had given them, letting out a long sigh of contentment.

“This, my dear Eleanor,” he said, gesturing around the room, “this is what it’s all for. To come home to this. To you.”

Eleanor smiled, wiping her hands on her apron as she came to sit on the armrest beside him, resting her head on his shoulder. “It is for both of us, Leo. This home, this life, we are building it together. And I could not be happier.”

“Nor I,” he murmured, pressing a kiss to her hair. “The work is challenging, of course, but it is deeply satisfying. To see my designs taking shape, to know that I am making a real contribution, it is everything I hoped for.” He paused, a faraway look in his eyes. “There is so much to do, Eleanor. So much to build, to improve. This city, this country, it is always moving forward, always striving for better. And I, I am eager to be a part of it.”

“And you will be, my brilliant Leo,” she said, her voice filled with admiration. “You already are.” She knew, with an absolute certainty, that their journey had just truly begun. They had found their foothold, secured their place. The vast, vibrant tapestry of New York stretched out before them, promising endless possibilities, and they, Leopold and Eleanor Fischer, were finally ready to weave their own thread into its magnificent design.
